OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Are there infinitely many $n$ (or any $n>105$) such that $n-2^k$ is prime for all $1<2^k<n$?
#1142: [Va99,1.7]
number theory | 
primes
The only known such $n$ are\[4,7,15,21,45,75,105.\]This is A039669 in the OEIS.
Mientka and Weitzenkamp [MiWe69] have proved there are no other such $n\leq 2^{44}$.
Vaughan [Va73] has proved that the number of $n\leq N$ such that $n-2^k$ is prime for all $1<2^k<n$ is\[< \exp\left(-c\frac{\log \log \log N}{\log\log N}\log N\right)N\]for some constant $c>0$.
This is discussed in problem A19 of Guy's collection [Gu04]. There is also further discussion on the Prime Puzzles website.
Erdős made the stronger conjecture (see [236]) that that number of $1<2^k<n$ for which $n-2^k$ is prime is $o(\log n)$.

 i checked all 2^120 <n < 2^128 and an OEIS comment suggests all n<2^120 have been checked. i used this algorithm (its AI-generated but i doubt its wrong, the code logic is pretty simple). It uses divisibility constraints derived on the prime puzzles website and a primality test. for this range, the divisibility was enough to rule all of them out. The run between 2^127 and 2^128 took about an hour on an M5 macbook, so it shouldn´t be that hard to improve with better hardware.

here, any proof of infinitely many such $n$ would imply infinitely many twin primes, so affirmatively proving this appears at least as hard as the twin prime conjecture.
